title: Scotland ended its council tax freeze — 22 of 32 hiked 8%+
narrative_md:
**After a year-long freeze funded by £144 million of retrospective Scottish Government money, Scottish households finally met the bill.**

At the 2023 SNP conference Humza Yousaf announced — to the surprise of finance directors across Scotland — a council tax freeze for 2024-25. Eighteen months later, with the freeze ended, 22 of Scotland's 32 councils imposed increases above 8%. Falkirk hit 15.6%.

The October 2023 freeze was political theatre with fiscal consequences. COSLA, Scotland's local-government umbrella body, had not been consulted. Finance secretaries from Labour, Lib Dem and independent-led councils accused the Scottish Government of announcing policy that was theirs to fund. After weeks of standoff, Holyrood committed £144 million of retrospective funding — roughly equivalent to a 5% council tax rise averaged across Scotland.

For 2025-26 the freeze was not repeated. Councils, facing years of suppressed tax bases, cost inflation and rising social-care demand, moved sharply: Falkirk +15.6%, Orkney +15%, Argyll and Bute +10%, Edinburgh +8%, Glasgow +7.5%. Only a handful — notably Inverclyde — held below 5%.

The underlying problem is that Scottish council tax is still calibrated to 1991 property valuations. A home assessed as Band D in 1991 pays Band D in 2026, regardless of whether its relative value has doubled or halved. The 2015 Commission on Local Tax Reform recommended replacing the system; successive Scottish Governments have declined. Wales revalued in 2003; England has not revalued since 1991 either. Scotland is therefore running a tax that is one year older than Sonic the Hedgehog.

A small but telling innovation is the Visitor Levy (Scotland) Act 2024, empowering councils to charge overnight visitors. Edinburgh became the first to adopt it, with a 5% levy on accommodation live from July 2026, forecast to raise £50 million a year. The levy is a political release valve — new revenue that avoids touching the untouchable council tax bands.

The General Resource Grant — the main Scottish Government transfer to councils — was increased by 4.4% for 2025-26, but real-terms it is still below 2013-14 levels. Much of the uplift is ring-fenced for teachers, social care or the Scottish Child Payment. Local discretion has narrowed. When the freeze ended, councils used the freedom they had: the council tax lever.

The politics are uncomfortable for the SNP. Voters who received a freeze in 2024 received double-digit rises in 2025; the Conservatives and Scottish Labour both campaigned on 'SNP freezes that unfreeze as tax hikes.' With Holyrood elections in May 2026, the council tax line will be contested ward by ward.

The longer-term question is whether any Scottish government will ever take the political cost of revaluation. Fifty years from 1991 falls in 2041. On current trends, that is the over/under.
